title: Notification system
summary: A shared push, email and SMS platform that keeps password resets fast while a campaign floods the pipe, and never sends twice from its own side.
interviewerPrompt: Our product teams each send their own push notifications, emails and texts, and it's a mess. Design a notification service they can all call instead. It needs to work at our scale.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Which channels, and do we build the delivery transport ourselves?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Mobile push, email and SMS, all delivered through third-party providers: APNs and FCM for push, one email provider and one SMS provider. Assume the providers' rate limits are about 100k/s for push, 10k/s for email and 1k/s for SMS.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How many users and how many notifications?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: 200M users and about 1B notifications a day, so roughly 11.6k per second on average.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the load steady or bursty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Bursty. Marketing campaigns to large segments cause 5× bursts over the average.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are all notifications equally important?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Transactional messages such as password resets, one-time codes and order updates must go out within seconds even while a campaign is running. Marketing can wait.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Who decides which channel a user gets?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The user. Respect per-category, per-channel preferences, global opt-outs and quiet hours in the user's time zone. Security messages ignore quiet hours.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How strict is 'no duplicates'?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The same notification must never be sent twice because of our retries or a caller retrying. Be explicit about what you can and cannot guarantee when a provider call times out.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What happens when a provider is slow or down?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The service must survive it: no lost notifications, no meltdown from retries, and urgent messages should still get out if there is a way.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do callers send one message at a time, or campaigns too?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Both. Product services send individual transactional messages; marketing sends one message to a segment of up to all users, optionally scheduled.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Who writes the message content?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Teams own versioned, localised templates; callers pass a template id and variables.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do callers need to know what happened?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes: they should be able to look up whether a notification was suppressed, sent, delivered or failed. An in-app inbox is out of scope.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should a user be protected from too many messages?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, cap marketing per user per day across all teams. Transactional messages are exempt.

deepDiveQuestions: How do you keep transactional messages fast during a 5× campaign burst?
How do retries, backoff and the dead-letter queue work, and what happens when a provider goes down?
What does 'never send twice' really mean, and where can duplicates still happen?
Where and how do you apply preferences, quiet hours and per-user rate limits?

runChallenge.title: Campaign burst with a zone down
runChallenge.description: Run a 5× campaign burst and lose the busiest availability zone after 10 s. The accept path must keep taking notifications with under 1% errors and a p99 under 200 ms, with no single point of failure.

commonMistakes: Putting transactional and marketing messages in one queue, so a campaign backlog delays password resets.
Scaling your own servers while ignoring that the providers' rate limits are the real bottleneck at peak.
Claiming exactly-once delivery to the provider instead of explaining the in-doubt timeout and a per-category retry policy.
Retrying every error the same way: retrying permanent failures such as invalid tokens, or retrying without backoff and jitter.
Checking preferences only at accept time, so an opt-out does not stop a campaign already in flight.
Letting retries block the main queue instead of using delayed retry queues and a dead-letter queue with an owner.
Forgetting expiry: retrying a one-time code or a 'driver is here' message long after it became useless.
No way to stop a campaign that was sent to the wrong segment.
